title: Simplex as walking between vertices (a tiny tableau implementation)

blocks.text: 2.2.2 Simplex as Walking Between Vertices (a Tiny Tableau Implementation)

Lesson 2.2.1 solved GridCap's budget split by listing every vertex of its region and keeping the best. That took ten pairs of lines for two variables; for a model with 100 variables and 200 rows the same count is about $`4 \times 10^{81}`$. GridCap's capital models are far bigger than that, and GLOP and HiGHS still solve their LPs. They do not list vertices. They start at one vertex and walk along the region's edges to a better neighbour, again and again, until no neighbour is better. That walk is the **simplex method** (George Dantzig, 1947), and it is the "S" in many solver logs.
This lesson builds the walk in about 60 lines of plain Python, runs it on the budget split, and watches it go A → B → C on the picture from lesson 2.2.1. It takes five rules.
The Model, With One Slack per Row
The budget split of lesson 2.2.1, unchanged: $`d`$ and $`t`$ are the money for distribution and transmission in $100k.

\begin{aligned}
\max \;& 5d + 4t \\
\text{s.t. }& d + t \le 30 && \text{(budget)} \\
& 3d + 2t \le 72 && \text{(crews)} \\
& t \le 20 && \text{(ready\_t)} \\
& d,\ t \ge 0
\end{aligned}

Simplex works with equations, not inequalities, so each $`\le`$ row gets a **slack variable**: a new variable that holds the row's unused amount (lesson 2.1.2 covers this conversion for every kind of row). The slack of budget, $`s_\text{budget}`$, is the money left unspent; $`s_\text{crews}`$ the crew-weeks left idle; $`s_\text{ready\_t}`$ the ready transmission work left undone. A slack can never be negative, since a negative slack would mean the row is broken:

\begin{aligned}
\max \;& 5d + 4t \\
\text{s.t. }& d + t + s_\text{budget} = 30 && \text{(budget)} \\
& 3d + 2t + s_\text{crews} = 72 && \text{(crews)} \\
& t + s_\text{ready\_t} = 20 && \text{(ready\_t)} \\
& d,\ t,\ s_\text{budget},\ s_\text{crews},\ s_\text{ready\_t} \ge 0
\end{aligned}

The two models have the same plans: a plan $`(d, t)`$ satisfies the first exactly when the slacks it defines are all $`\ge 0`$ in the second. Now there are $`n = 2`$ original variables, $`m = 3`$ equations, and $`n + m = 5`$ variables in all.
A Vertex Is a Basis: Set n Variables to Zero and Solve for the Rest

Three equations can pin down three unknowns. So pick any 2 of the 5 variables, set them to 0, and solve the three equations for the other 3. The 3 you solve for are the **basic** variables, and the set of them is the **basis**; the 2 you set to zero are **nonbasic**. The point you get is a **basic solution**.

A slack at 0 means its row is tight, and $`d = 0`$ or $`t = 0`$ means a bound is tight. So setting 2 variables to zero is choosing 2 tight rows, which is exactly how lesson 2.2.1 found the crossing points. Three bases, solved:

A basic solution whose values are all $`\ge 0`$ is a **basic feasible solution**, and the basic feasible solutions are exactly the vertices. A basic solution with a negative value is one of the crossings outside the region. Making $`s_\text{budget}`$ and $`d`$ nonbasic, for example, gives $`t = 30`$, $`s_\text{crews} = 72 - 60 = 12`$ and $`s_\text{ready\_t} = 20 - 30 = -10`$: the crossing at $`(0, 30)`$ that lesson 2.2.1 found breaks ready_t.

Two vertices are **neighbours**, joined by an edge of the region, when their bases differ in one variable: A and B share the basic variables $`s_\text{budget}`$ and $`s_\text{ready\_t}`$, and differ only in whether $`s_\text{crews}`$ or $`d`$ is the third. One step of simplex swaps one variable into the basis and one out: the **entering** variable rises from 0, and the **leaving** variable falls to 0.
The Tableau Holds the Equations, and Its Last Row Says Which Variable Improves the Objective

A **tableau** is the equations written as a table of numbers: one row per equation, one column per variable, and a last column for the right-hand sides. Below them sits one more row for the objective. Write the objective's value as $`z`$, so $`z = 5d + 4t`$, and move every variable to the left: $`z - 5d - 4t = 0`$. The objective row stores the coefficients $`-5, -4, 0, 0, 0`$ and the current value of $`z`$ on the right.

def tableau(A: list[list[float]], b: list[float], c: list[float]) -> list[list[float]]:
    m = len(A)
    rows = [list(map(float, A[i])) + [1.0 if j == i else 0.0 for j in range(m)] + [float(b[i])]
            for i in range(m)]
    return rows + [[-float(cj) for cj in c] + [0.0] * m + [0.0]]

Row $`i`$ is the row $`i`$ of $`A`$, then a 1 in the column of slack $`i`$ and 0 for the other slacks, then $`b_i`$. The last row is $`-c`$, zeros under the slacks, and 0 for $`z`$. Built for the budget split and printed:

A = [list(a) for a, _ in ROWS.values()]
b = [rhs for _, rhs in ROWS.values()]
names = list(NAMES) + [f"s_{label}" for label in ROWS]
T = tableau(A, b, VALUE)
basis = list(range(len(NAMES), len(names)))
show(T, names, basis)

basis         d         t  s_budget   s_crews s_ready_t       rhs
 s_budget         1         1         1         0         0        30
  s_crews         3         2         0         1         0        72
s_ready_t         0         1         0         0         1        20
objective        -5        -4         0         0         0         0

Each basic variable's column is a **unit column**: a 1 in its own row and 0 everywhere else, including the objective row. That is what makes a tableau easy to read. Set the nonbasic variables to 0 and each row says "this basic variable equals the right-hand side". So the tableau is at vertex A: $`d = t = 0`$, the slacks hold 30, 72 and 20, and $`z = 0`$.

The objective row reads the same way. Written out, it says $`z - 5d - 4t = 0`$, that is $`z = 0 + 5d + 4t`$: raising nonbasic $`d`$ from 0 adds 5 to $`z`$ per unit, and raising $`t`$ adds 4. In general, the objective row always says
z = \text{(rhs of the objective row)} - \sum_{j \text{ nonbasic}} (\text{entry}_j)\, x_j

so **a negative entry marks a variable that improves the objective if it enters**. These entries are the **reduced costs** of the nonbasic variables (lesson 2.3.3 reads them from a solver). Which negative entry to pick is a choice; the classic rule, **Dantzig's rule**, takes the most negative:

def entering(T: list[list[float]]) -> int | None:
    """The column with the most negative entry in the objective row; None when none improves."""
    z = T[-1][:-1]
    k = min(range(len(z)), key=lambda j: z[j])
    return k if z[k] < -EPS else None
`EPS` is $`10^{-9}`$: an entry like $`-10^{-15}`$ is float noise, not a real improvement. Here the most negative entry is $`-5`$, so $`d`$ enters.
The Ratio Test Picks the Row That Leaves: the First Basic Variable to Reach Zero
$`d`$ rises from 0 while $`t`$ stays 0. Each equation then says how a basic variable must change to keep the equation true:
s_\text{budget} = 30 - 1 \cdot d, \qquad s_\text{crews} = 72 - 3d, \qquad s_\text{ready\_t} = 20 - 0 \cdot d

Every basic variable must stay $`\ge 0`$. $`s_\text{budget}`$ reaches 0 at $`d = 30`$, $`s_\text{crews}`$ at $`d = 72/3 = 24`$, and $`s_\text{ready\_t}`$ never does. So $`d`$ can rise to 24 and no further: one unit more and $`s_\text{crews}`$ would be negative, which means the plan would need more crew-weeks than exist. $`s_\text{crews}`$ is the leaving variable.

That is the **ratio test**: for every row whose entry in the entering column is positive, divide the right-hand side by that entry, and pick the row with the smallest ratio. A row whose entry is zero or negative sets no limit, because raising the entering variable leaves its basic variable unchanged or makes it larger. Ties go to the lowest row here; any tied row is a correct choice.

def leaving(T: list[list[float]], k: int) -> int | None:
    """The ratio test: the row whose b_i / a_ik is smallest over a_ik > 0; None when no row limits k."""
    ratios = [(T[i][-1] / T[i][k], i) for i in range(len(T) - 1) if T[i][k] > EPS]
    return min(ratios)[1] if ratios else None

The smallest ratio is the step length: how far the entering variable rises. When no row has a positive entry, nothing stops the rise; lesson 2.2.3 shows what that means. The walk program prints its test:

entering d: its objective-row entry is -5
  ratio test, row s_budget: 30 divided by 1 is 30
  ratio test, row s_crews: 72 divided by 3 is 24
  ratio test, row s_ready_t: entry 0, sets no limit
leaving s_crews

Taking the smallest ratio is what keeps the walk inside the region. Picking budget's 30 instead would push $`d`$ to 30, and the plan $`(30, 0)`$ needs 90 crew-weeks: it is the crossing that lesson 2.2.1 found "outside: breaks crews".
<!-- practice 1 -->
A Pivot Rewrites the Tableau So the Entering Variable Is Basic

The tableau must now describe vertex B, with $`d`$ basic in the row $`s_\text{crews}`$ held. That means turning $`d`$'s column into a unit column with its 1 in that row. The operation is a **pivot**, on the **pivot element** where the leaving row meets the entering column (here the 3). It uses the two row operations that never change what a system of equations means:

items: Divide the pivot row by the pivot element, so the pivot element becomes 1.
From every other row, objective row included, subtract the new pivot row times that row's entry in the pivot column, so the entry becomes 0.

blocks.text:
def pivot(T: list[list[float]], r: int, k: int) -> list[list[float]]:
    """Make column k a unit column with its 1 in row r: one step to a neighbouring vertex."""
    row = [v / T[r][k] for v in T[r]]
    return [row if i == r else [v - T[i][k] * w for v, w in zip(T[i], row)] for i in range(len(T))]
`pivot` returns a new tableau and leaves the old one as it was. After the pivot:

basis         d         t  s_budget   s_crews s_ready_t       rhs
 s_budget         0       1/3         1      -1/3         0         6
        d         1       2/3         0       1/3         0        24
s_ready_t         0         1         0         0         1        20
objective         0      -2/3         0       5/3         0       120

Read it as before. $`d = 24`$, $`s_\text{budget} = 6`$ (that is $600k unspent), $`s_\text{ready\_t} = 20`$, and the nonbasic $`t`$ and $`s_\text{crews}`$ are 0. That is vertex B, worth 120, and the right-hand side of the objective row says so. The step moved along one edge of the region, from A to B, along the bottom edge $`t = 0`$.
<!-- practice 2 -->
When No Objective-Row Entry Is Negative, the Vertex Is Optimal

The objective row at B reads $`z = 120 + \tfrac{2}{3} t - \tfrac{5}{3} s_\text{crews}`$. Raising $`t`$ still pays $`\tfrac{2}{3}`$ per unit. That is less than the 4 that $`t`$ earned at A, because at B raising $`t`$ must lower $`d`$ to free crew-weeks: each unit of $`t`$ uses 2 crew-weeks, which costs $`\tfrac{2}{3}`$ of a unit of $`d`$, worth $`\tfrac{10}{3}`$, so the net is $`4 - \tfrac{10}{3} = \tfrac{2}{3}`$. The reduced cost counts that trade automatically. So $`t`$ enters, and the walk continues:

entering t: its objective-row entry is -2/3
  ratio test, row s_budget: 6 divided by 1/3 is 18
  ratio test, row d: 24 divided by 2/3 is 36
  ratio test, row s_ready_t: 20 divided by 1 is 20
leaving s_budget
    basis         d         t  s_budget   s_crews s_ready_t       rhs
        t         0         1         3        -1         0        18
        d         1         0        -2         1         0        12
s_ready_t         0         0        -3         1         1         2
objective         0         0         2         1         0       132
The budget runs out first, at $`t = 18`$. The tableau is now at vertex C: $`d = 12`$, $`t = 18`$, $`s_\text{ready\_t} = 2`$, value 132. Its objective row has no negative entry, and it says
z = 132 - 2\, s_\text{budget} - 1\, s_\text{crews}

That one line is a proof that C is optimal. It is an equation that every feasible plan satisfies, since the tableau is the original equations rearranged. Every feasible plan has $`s_\text{budget} \ge 0`$ and $`s_\text{crews} \ge 0`$, so every feasible plan has $`z \le 132`$, and C reaches 132. This is the **optimality test**: when no entry of the objective row is negative, no neighbour is better, and by the argument just given no plan anywhere is. Because the region is convex, a vertex that beats its neighbours is the best overall: an LP has no "local best" that is not the global best.

The two numbers in the slack columns also have a meaning the planner cares about. Leaving one unit ($100k) of budget unspent costs 2 risk points; leaving one crew-week idle costs 1. Lessons 2.3.1 and 2.3.3 call them **dual values** (or shadow prices) and show what they say about buying more budget or crews.
Put together, the walk is a loop: find an entering column, run the ratio test, pivot, repeat until the optimality test passes.

`basis[i]` is the column of the variable basic in row `i`, and `point` reads every basic variable's value off the right-hand side. The `UNBOUNDED` branch and `max_steps` are for lesson 2.2.3. Run on the budget split:

d enters, s_crews leaves, step 24: vertex (24, 0), value 120
t enters, s_budget leaves, step 18: vertex (12, 18), value 132
OPTIMAL: d = 12, t = 18, value 132

Two pivots, A → B → C, the same answer as the picture and as GLOP in lesson 2.2.1. On the map of lesson 2.2.1, the walk ran along the bottom edge and then up the crews line. It never looked at D or E.
Nothing in `solve` is about two variables. OR-Tools' MathOpt sample `linear_programming.py` (lesson 2.1.1 read its answer) has three, so its region is a solid, no longer a polygon on paper:
Its rows go into the tableau as they are, and GLOP solves the same LP for comparison:
result = solve(A, b, c, NAMES + ["s_c1", "s_c2", "s_c3"])

x0 enters, s_c1 leaves, step 60: vertex (60, 0, 0), value 600
x1 enters, s_c3 leaves, step 200/3: vertex (100/3, 200/3, 0), value 2200/3
tableau OPTIMAL: x = (100/3, 200/3, 0), value 2200/3
GLOP    OPTIMAL: x = (33.3333, 66.6667, 0.0000), value 733.3333

Two pivots again, to the vertex GLOP returns. The first ratio test compared c1's $`600 / 10 = 60`$, c2's $`300 / 2 = 150`$ and c3's $`100 / 1 = 100`$, so c1 left the basis first. At the end, $`x_0`$, $`x_1`$ and the slack of c2 are basic, one per row, and c1 and c3 are the tight rows that lesson 2.1.1 found full.

This tableau needs every $`b_i \ge 0`$, so that the slack basis at the origin is feasible. GridCap's real rows include $`\ge`$ commitments, for which the origin is not feasible; lesson 2.2.3 shows how a solver finds its first vertex then.
Summary

items: **A vertex is a basis.** Add a slack to every row; set $`n`$ of the $`n + m`$ variables to zero and solve for the rest. If every value is $`\ge 0`$, the point is a vertex.
**The tableau's last row says which variable improves the objective.** A negative entry (reduced cost) marks a nonbasic variable whose increase raises $`z`$; Dantzig's rule picks the most negative.
**The ratio test picks the row that leaves:** the smallest $`b_i / a_{ik}`$ over rows with $`a_{ik} > 0`$, the first basic variable to reach zero. It keeps the walk inside the region.
**A pivot rewrites the tableau so the entering variable is basic**, with two row operations, and moves to a neighbouring vertex.
**When no objective-row entry is negative, the vertex is optimal.** The objective row is then a proof: $`z`$ equals the current value minus nonnegative terms.

blocks.text: Reference

rows: unused amount of row $`i`$: $`s_i = b_i - a_i \cdot x \ge 0`$
the $`m`$ variables solved for; the other $`n`$ (nonbasic) are 0
a basic solution with every value $`\ge 0`$; the same thing as a vertex
$`[A \mid I \mid b]`$ over $`[-c \mid 0 \mid z]`$ for $`\max c \cdot x`$, $`Ax \le b`$, $`x \ge 0`$, $`b \ge 0`$
a nonbasic column's objective-row entry; negative means entering improves $`z`$
Dantzig's rule: the most negative objective-row entry
divide row $`r`$ by $`a_{rk}`$; subtract $`a_{ik}`$ times it from every other row $`i`$
no negative entry in the objective row

blocks.text: **Further reading:** [MathOpt sample linear_programming.py](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/math_opt/samples/python/linear_programming.py) (the three-variable LP walked above); [Advanced LP Solving (OR-Tools)](https://developers.google.com/optimization/lp/lp_advanced) (primal simplex steps along vertices of the plan's region, dual simplex along those of the prices', and GLOP is Google's implementation of both); [Vanderbei, *Linear Programming: Foundations and Extensions*](https://vanderbei.princeton.edu/LPbook/) (the textbook's page, with its [Simple Pivot Tool](https://vanderbei.princeton.edu/JAVA/pivot/simple.html): pivot a random LP by hand in the book's dictionary form, with every primal and dual infeasible entry highlighted until the dictionary is optimal).
Challenges

items: Use the other entering rule: let $`t`$ enter first at A (its entry is negative too). Which vertices does the walk visit, and is it longer or shorter?

In the final tableau, the row of $`s_\text{ready\_t}`$ says $`s_\text{ready\_t} - 3 s_\text{budget} + s_\text{crews} = 2`$. Use it to say how much more ready transmission work would be left undone if $100k of the budget were left unspent and the crews stayed fully used.
Why can simplex never visit the same vertex twice when every step length is positive? (Lesson 2.2.3 shows the case where a step length is zero.)

blocks.text: Design Note: Why Real Solvers Do Not Store a Tableau

This tableau is dense: every pivot rewrites all $`(m + 1)(n + m + 1)`$ numbers, most of which are zeros in a real model (lesson 1.2.2). Production simplex codes keep the original sparse matrix and a factorization of the current basis instead, and compute only the one column and one row a pivot needs. That variant is called the **revised simplex method**. The walk is the same: same bases, same ratio test, same optimality test, and the 60 lines here are a faithful small model of it. GLOP, OR-Tools' simplex code, implements both the primal simplex of this lesson and the dual simplex that lesson 2.4.1 describes. Lesson 2.4.1 also compares simplex with methods that do not walk between vertices: interior point methods, which cross the inside of the region, and first-order methods such as PDLP, which take many small steps on the plan and the prices together.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.

**simplex_walk.py.** Builds the budget split's tableau, prints the ratio test and the tableau at every pivot, then runs `solve` and lists the vertices it visited (every section of this lesson). *Try:* Change `VALUE` in `split_lp.py` to `(5, 6)`. Predict the first entering variable and the number of pivots, then run it.

**simplex_sample.py.** Adapted from the OR-Tools MathOpt sample `linear_programming.py`: the tableau simplex walks its three-variable LP, and GLOP solves it for comparison (*When No Objective-Row Entry Is Negative*). *Try:* Change c to `[10, 6, 9]`. Predict which variable enters first and whether $`x_2`$ stays at 0.
**simplex.py.** The tableau simplex itself: `tableau`, `entering`, `leaving`, `pivot` and `solve`, plus `show` and `fmt` to print a tableau with fractions.
